inline.s: After he sat upright and passed away, in accordance with the Buddha's rule he was placed in a shrine, cremated, and his ashes placed in a stupa. When all these matters were done it was already the middle of the sixth month. Time flew like a galloping horse, and in a flash the seventh, eighth, and ninth months passed, yet there was no news at all. I privately supposed that the layperson had not been reborn in the West, or that having been reborn there he was unwilling to communicate with us, so that the agreement we had made could not be fulfilled. But contrary
(unexpectedly)
to expectations, at the end of the eleventh month
(the end of the eleventh month of the lunar calendar)

on one day, Mr. Wang, owing to a toothache, lay down to rest upon his bed in the daytime. In a drowse he saw the layperson ascend the stairs and sit upon a stool. (Original note: Because Mr. Wang practiced Buddha-recitation, his bed was placed beside the recitation hall upstairs.) His frame was as before, wearing a nearly new flat-topped hat and clothes that seemed to have been freshly washed — all clean, with a radiance emanating from them. His spirit was bright and untrammeled, his face like the full moon. His skin was tender and delicate, like that of a handsome eight-year-old boy. Compared with his living face, full of moustache and beard
(whiskers)
, with teeth fallen out and skin wrinkled, he was as if a different man. Had Mr. Wang not been his closest friend, acquainted
(intimately familiar)
with him to the fullest, and moreover a childhood friend of the same village
(a friend made in boyhood)
, he would hardly have been able to recognize him. For this beautiful bearing was something the layperson had never had in all his life.
At the first sight Mr. Wang was extraordinarily startled and delighted, and spoke without order, hastily
(abruptly)

asking: ‘Ah! Have you in truth been reborn in the West? If not, how could you have such grace? You do not know how your face now is — altogether a tender, handsome boy. When you were alive most of your teeth had fallen; I once promised you to go to Pine and Bamboo Studio to have your teeth set. Do you still remember?’ The layperson said: ‘Yes, yes, I have made a point of coming to tell you the news.’ Mr. Wang said: ‘The West is one hundred thousand million Buddha-lands away from here; it is not easy to reach at all. How did you manage to get there?’ He answered: ‘That I got there was entirely the power of faith and vow.’ Mr. Wang said: ‘How were you able to go?’ He answered: ‘Very easy — at the very raising of a single thought I was there. In time you will know for yourself. Only, when coming, look toward the dark place, and when going, look toward the bright place — that is all.’ Mr. Wang asked again: ‘Have you seen the Buddha?’ He answered: ‘Not yet.’ He asked: ‘Why could you not see him?’ He answered: ‘My merit and practice were too shallow, so I was not born in the pool of the seven jewels.’ He asked: ‘Not born in the pool of the seven jewels — then where were you born?’ The layperson sighed: ‘Alas, the place I went to was only the ground of the West. Ah, I suppose it counts as the borderlands.’

Before the conversation was finished, of a sudden he woke. Opening his eyes and recalling, he felt that the layperson's speech and bearing, and the radiant mark and good form, stood clearly before his eyes — in no way to be compared to the inverted thoughts of a dream. Rising to look at the clock, it was just a little past five in the afternoon. A month later
(after a month had passed)

, when the twelfth month had ended and spring had returned, Mr. Wang chanced to meet the layperson's relative Wang Nengzhi. The moment they met, Nengzhi at once said to Mr. Wang: ‘Strange! Last winter Zhu Xingwu came several times to talk with me, saying that he had attained the borderlands of the West and had come specially to deliver the news. I have long wished to visit you to tell you of it all.’ Mr. Wang, eagerly
(urgently)

finding out what he had said, Nengzhi related: ‘The moment I saw him I asked: Where did you go these past few months? Why did you not come earlier? The layperson answered: Because I had some business in the underworld, I was delayed a long while. Thanks to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva's sending someone to escort me, I was only then able to spare a moment to come. He also said: When I was alive I gave you books on Buddha-recitation — did you put them into practice? In the past you ran an eatery and did much slaughter; your wrongdoing is very heavy. From now on, besides earnestly reciting the Buddha-name, you must further repent, become a vegetarian, and strictly observe the precept against killing. As for rebirth in the West, everyone has a share in it; it is very easy, so do not on any account give yourself up. I greatly regret that I began to recite too late and that my merit was too poor; you should begin your practice early — that is the point, and so on.’ After the layperson had delivered the news, Mr. Wang's friends, hearing of it, urged him to record it to awaken people's faith. Mr. Wang thereupon wrote it out directly as the matter had occurred. And in an afterword he wrote: ‘I solemnly swear by my precepts that there is not a single false word, and that I have not changed a single word, more or less, of what Mr. Zhu said in the dream.’ Recently he sent a letter to this journal and asked that it be published. All now relate this account, to inform the monastics and laypeople of the whole country.
July
Honghua Monthly, no.
Zhanran

The power of example is boundless! The above examples of free and unhindered rebirth are immensely inspiring and also give one much to ponder. Han Yu, in his essay On the Root of Fault-Finding, has a passage telling people how to use examples to improve themselves:

“I heard that among the ancients there was one Shun, and in his way of being he was a man of benevolence and righteousness. Seeking the principle by which Shun became Shun, one blames oneself, saying: ‘He is a man; I too am a man. He was able to be this, and can I not be this?’ Morning and night one ponders, discarding what is not like Shun and taking up what is like Shun.”

(Vernacular: I hear that among the ancients there was one called Shun, and his conduct was that of a man of benevolence and righteousness. Having found the principle by which Shun became Shun, one blames oneself, saying: ‘He is a man, and I too am a man; he was able to be thus, am I then unable to be thus?’ So morning and night one thinks of how to catch up — discarding those places where one is not like Shun, and imitating those places where one is like Shun.)

When we read these examples of free rebirth, we too should thus blame ourselves, and ponder morning and night, discarding what is not like them and taking up what is like them. Yet in the accounts of free rebirth handed down through the ages, often there is only the matter of the deed, without setting forth the state he had reached before his passing, or how he came to that state — making it hard for people to emulate;
this is indeed a matter of great regret!

Take the matter of “Wei Guoxing's free rebirth” as an example. He had been reciting the Buddha's name only a mere three or five years when he foresaw that he would pass away at noon, twelve o'clock, seven days later. So he informed the practice-place in advance, and the practice-place held a grand seven-day Dharma-gathering of rebirth-and-Buddha for more than fifteen hundred people, chanting to see him off. If in these seven days someone had carefully questioned him about the state he had reached at that time, and how he had come to that state, and published it to the world, how immense would have been the help to those practicing Buddha-recitation!

I earnestly hope that those so fortunate as to meet in the future a person who foresees the time of his passing will carefully question him as to his state and how he reached it, and make it known to all, for the benefit of the practitioners of Buddha-recitation in all ages to come. If a practitioner of Buddha-recitation has foreknowledge of his time, then before he passes away let him, with a bodhi-mind, tell his fellow practitioners his concrete methods of study and practice, the process, and the states he attained, together with his experiences and lessons — or write them up for publication — and thus, before the fulfillment of his vow to return, broadly ferry sentient beings across.
